summary: Defines methods to manage OAuth 2.0 dynamic client registrations, for cases where a registered client's properties change over time. Not all servers need to support it. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: After getting a badge, you can come back to update your details or hand it back.

questions: how do i update my oauth client registration
how do i delete an oauth client
what is the client configuration endpoint
subtitle: Methods to manage OAuth 2.0 client registrations throughout their lifetime.

tldr.problem: Once an OAuth 2.0 client is registered with an authorization server, there is no standard way to read, update, or remove its registration as circumstances change.
tldr.mechanism: This specification adds a client configuration endpoint where a client can authenticate with a registration access token to read its current registration, submit updates, or delete itself entirely.
tldr.outcome: Clients can now manage their registrations dynamically, enabling credential rotation and deprovisioning. The specification is experimental to encourage implementation feedback.

today: RFC 7592 is experimental, published to encourage development of interoperable client management solutions. It remains the primary standard for dynamic management of OAuth 2.0 client registrations.

sections.title: The Problem with Static Registrations
sections.content:
OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) lets a client program register itself with an authorization server to get a client identifier and credentials. But that RFC assumes the registration is static once created. In reality, client properties change: software gets updated, credentials need rotating, or a client simply goes out of service.

This specification adds three new operations to manage dynamic registrations: reading the current configuration, updating it with new values, and deleting the client entirely. All three use a registration access token that the authorization server issues when the client first registers, and a new endpoint called the client configuration endpoint.
sections.plainLanguage: Some programs need to change their registration after they sign up, or delete their account. This spec describes how to do that safely using a special token.

sections.title: The Client Configuration Endpoint
sections.content:
The authorization server returns a registration_client_uri (the client configuration endpoint URL) and a registration_access_token when the client first registers. The client uses these together for all three operations.

Read Request: A client sends an HTTP GET to the endpoint, authenticated with the registration access token as a Bearer Token. The server responds with HTTP 200 and the full current configuration in JSON, which may include new values for the client secret and registration access token.

Update Request: A client sends an HTTP PUT with a JSON body containing all client metadata fields. The client must include its client_id and match its current client_secret. Omitted fields are treated as deleted. The server responds with HTTP 200 and the updated configuration, potentially with new credentials.

Delete Request: A client sends an HTTP DELETE to deregister itself. The server responds with HTTP 204 No Content and invalidates the client_id, client_secret, and all associated tokens.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoint lets you ask 'what is my current setup?', 'here is my new information', or 'please delete me'. Each request is signed with a special token that proves it is really you.

sections.title: Client Information Response
sections.content:
When a client reads or updates its configuration, the authorization server responds with a JSON object containing two required new fields: registration_client_uri (the fully qualified endpoint URL for this client) and registration_access_token (the Bearer Token to use on the next request).

The response must also include all registered metadata about the client, including any fields the authorization server generated itself. The server may reject or replace invalid metadata values with suitable defaults and return the final values to the client.

If the server issues a new registration access token, it replaces the old one; the client must discard the old token immediately. The client_id must never change from the original registration.
sections.plainLanguage: The server always sends back your current settings and a fresh token to use next time. If your information was wrong or forbidden, the server replaces it with something safe.

sections.title: Security and Credential Rotation
sections.content:
The registration access token is a long-term credential and must be protected as a Bearer Token (RFC 6750): treat it as a secret and never share it between client instances. The token should not expire while the client is actively registered, because expiry would lock out the developer.

All requests to the client configuration endpoint must use transport-layer security (TLS 1.2 or higher), since they transmit credentials in the clear. The client must verify the server certificate per RFC 6125.

The registration access token must contain enough entropy to prevent random guessing attacks. The server may rotate the registration access token or client credentials during any read or update operation to minimize the impact of leaks, but only in response to a client request.

If a client is deprovisioned, the server must immediately invalidate all outstanding registration access tokens for that client and all associated authorization grants, access tokens, and refresh tokens.
sections.plainLanguage: Treat your token like a password: keep it secret, use a secure connection, and never share it. The server can give you a fresh token anytime to reduce the damage if the old one leaks.

sections.title: Relationship to Core Registration
sections.content:
This specification extends RFC 7591 (OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Protocol), which defines how a client first registers. RFC 7591 does not define management of existing registrations; this document fills that gap.

Authorization servers are not required to implement these management methods. Some servers may support only registration or only a subset of the three operations. A server that does not support a particular HTTP method on the client configuration endpoint MUST respond with an appropriate error code (such as HTTP 405 Method Not Allowed).

The specification includes practical guidance on credential rotation and on how to form the client configuration endpoint URL, but these are recommendations rather than requirements, allowing servers flexibility in deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a follow-up to the original registration spec. Not all servers have to implement these features, and servers can support different combinations of read, update, or delete.
